You're working on Nxeon, a hosting platform (Next.js/TypeScript/Prisma/Postgres) running on a Proxmox server. `/opt/nxeon` is production (git, origin/main). You have shell access to the same host that runs the actual game-server VMs.

## The task

The owner asked: "verify the health of all of the new servers that got deployed today and see if there are any bugs to fix for future deployments." I already did the first pass — only 2 servers were created today (2026-08-28): `mobilkit` (a VPS, healthy, no errors) and `rust-w75hko` (a Rust game server, id `cmtd2ebgs12yahluy6d6vmcan`, owned by user `jasminemorrell23@gmail.com`) which has TWO real, confirmed problems. Your job: root-cause both, fix what's fixable, and specifically look for anything that would repeat on FUTURE deployments (not just patch this one customer's server).

## What I already found — don't re-derive this, start from here

1. **The game process never came up during provisioning.** The `PROVISION` job (id `cmtd2ebgw12ychluy9xb8973h`) completed with `status: "DONE"` but has a non-null `error` field: `"game port 28016/tcp never opened on 10.20.0.105 after ~300s (31 attempt(s); last error: ECONNREFUSED). SSH is up, but the game server itself never started listening, so this server cannot be handed to the customer as ready."` — meaning the VM itself came up fine (SSH worked), but the actual Rust game server process never bound its port. The job was still marked DONE despite this error being attached, and the customer's `Server.status` is `RUNNING` — so the customer likely sees "running" while the game itself may not actually be playable. Find where this provisioning error gets set (grep worker/index.ts and worker/game-*.ts for "never opened" / "cannot be handed to the customer") and: (a) confirm whether a DONE job with a non-null error actually surfaces this to the customer anywhere in the UI right now (check `app/dashboard/servers/[id]/page.tsx` and whatever renders game-server status) — if it's silently swallowed, that's the first bug to fix; (b) figure out WHY the Rust process didn't start — check the actual VM (you have shell access to the host; the server's internal IP is `10.20.0.105`, SSH port `20008` per the DB — the exact SSH connection mechanics are in `lib/sftp.ts`/`worker/game-control.ts`'s `withServerSsh` helper, read it to find the right way to connect) — look for the game's systemd unit / docker container status, its actual startup logs, and see if this is a one-off flake (e.g. a slow image pull that would have succeeded past the 300s timeout) or a real, reproducible provisioning defect for the Rust family specifically.

2. **All later `GAME_POWER` actions (5 of them, between 15:27 and 16:01 today) failed with "All configured authentication methods failed"** — an SSH auth rejection, NOT a timeout. This happened AFTER the provisioning SSH connection had already worked. Investigate: did something about the stored credential (`rootPassword` vs `rootPasswordEnc` — this server has both fields, check which one `withServerSsh` actually reads and whether they're consistent) change or desync between provisioning time and these later power-action attempts? Or did the VM's sshd itself start rejecting (check for fail2ban or similar on the VM, check actual sshd logs on the VM if you can reach it via the Proxmox host's console/qm tool even if SSH itself is currently rejecting). This node/IP detail is also unusual: `Server.nodeId` is `null` for this server (I confirmed this directly) — check whether that's normal for how this shared-IP/NAT game-server path assigns nodes (grep for how game servers on the shared-IP path get their `nodeId`, or whether a null `nodeId` here is ITSELF a bug that could explain the SSH routing failing later — e.g. if some later code path needs `server.node` to resolve the SSH target and silently falls back to something wrong when it's null).

## Scope — be honest, not heroic

- If this looks like a one-off environmental flake (e.g. a transient Docker Hub pull failure, a slow node under load at that specific moment) that isn't likely to repeat, say so clearly and don't invent a speculative fix for a problem that may not be systemic.
- If you find a REAL, reproducible defect (e.g. the null `nodeId` genuinely breaks later SSH routing for any NAT/shared-IP game server, or the Rust family's control spec / systemd unit detection has a real bug), fix it properly — this is exactly the "bugs to fix for future deployments" the owner asked about.
- For THIS specific customer's broken server: once you understand the actual state (is the Rust process actually running or not, right now), decide whether to attempt a live fix (e.g. a manual restart via the Proxmox host once you understand why SSH auth is failing) so the customer isn't left with a broken paid service, or whether that needs the owner's involvement — use your judgment, but don't leave a paying customer's server silently broken without at least a clear status in your report.
- Check whether OTHER existing (not just today's) game servers on this platform have `nodeId: null` too — if it's widespread, that's a bigger, pre-existing issue worth flagging even if unrelated to "today's deployments" specifically; if it's just this one, say so.

## Verification discipline (for any code fix)
1. Baseline: `cd /opt/nxeon && npm test 2>&1 | grep "^not ok"` before changes (34 pre-existing failures expected).
2. `npx tsc --noEmit` clean after any change.
3. `npm test` failure set identical to baseline after.
4. Commit ending in:
   ```

   Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
   ```
   `git push origin main` — retry once after 2s on "cannot lock ref" (transient, other work lands on main concurrently from elsewhere in this session).
5. Deploy any fix to staging (`bash scripts/deploy-staging.sh main`) and verify there before considering it done — do NOT run `scripts/promote-production.sh`, staging only.
6. If you make any LIVE intervention on the actual customer's VM (restarting a service, fixing SSH access) to unblock their broken paid service, that's a production infrastructure action outside the normal staging-first code-change flow — be careful, document exactly what you did and why, and don't do anything destructive (no VM recreation, no data loss) without stopping to report back first if you're unsure.

## Final report
The root cause of both issues (or your best evidence-based finding if inconclusive), whether this server is fixed and the customer can actually play right now, whether you found or fixed a systemic bug that would affect future Rust/game-server deployments, the `nodeId: null` finding's scope (this server only, or widespread), and any judgment calls.
